summary: Discovery/POC scoping focused on cost modeling and unit economics for a 6-week POC. Discussed workload sizing (tokens per request, concurrency), batching/caching knobs, hosted vs dedicated tradeoffs, target latency SLOs, and next steps to run benchmarks and share SOW/pricing.
topics: workload sizing: RPS, concurrency, tokens per request
benchmarks: p50/p95 latency, throughput, token cost
batching and KV/prefix caching effects on unit economics
pricing scenarios: hosted API vs dedicated reserved capacity
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Patel (Redwood AE): Alright everyone thanks for joining, we're on the call to scope the POC around cost modeling and unit economics. I see Lena, Tom, Priya - thanks for your time. Carlos from our SE team is here as well. Quick agenda: run through current workload, success criteria, sizing, then benchmarks and pricing assumptions.

[00:28] Tom Rivers (CTO, Aperture): Yep thanks Maya. High level - we're evaluating options to power a real-time insights feature in our analytics product. Primary concern is cost at scale and predictable latency. We have about 600k MAU today, peak 300 RPS across endpoints, but only a subset hit the LLM pipe.

[01:02] Lena Chen (Head of ML Ops): To add, typical call is 1.2k tokens on average for the full multi-turn context, worst case 4k tokens. We do a mix of short prompts and long summarizations. Our SLA target is 300ms p50, 900ms p95 for the critical endpoint.

[01:25] Carlos Gomez (Redwood SE): Great - that helps. A couple clarifying Qs: when you say 300 RPS peak, how many concurrent LLM sessions does that translate to? And what's your acceptable cost per 1k tokens?

[01:42] Priya Nair (DevOps): We estimate about 120 concurrent LLM sessions at peak. For cost, leadership wants a model that does not exceed roughly $0.02 per 1k tokens served in steady state - arbitrary target but that's the budget ceiling.

[02:05] Maya: Good. So scope for the POC: validate feasibility to meet latency SLOs and demonstrate unit economics under sample workload. We'll run hosted tests first, then a dedicated baseline if needed. Acceptance criteria? Latency p95 under 1s, token cost within target or clear path to it with batching/quantization, and no blocking security gaps.

[02:35] Tom: That sounds reasonable. Walk us through how batching and caching will materially affect the per-token cost.

[02:44] Carlos: Sure. Two knobs that move the needle: batching (amortize GPU kernel overhead across requests) and prefix/KV caching (avoid recomputing left context for repeated prompts). For your mix (avg 1.2k tokens), caching will help for repeated templates; batching helps for concurrency spikes. Quantization and model choice (e.g., 7B vs 13B or quantized 4-bit) changes token throughput/latency and cost too.

[03:10] Lena: Our prompts include a stable system prompt + user content; we do see a lot of repeated system-level tokens so KV caching could cut costs. But some endpoints require full context each time, so not everything caches.

[03:27] Maya: For cost modeling we typically produce two scenarios: conservative (minimal caching, smaller batch sizes) and optimized (aggressive caching + batching + int8/4 quantization). We'll run benchmarks for your representative prompts to estimate per-token cost.

[03:45] Priya: How do you instrument cost per token? Do you include infra amortization for dedicated?

[03:52] Carlos: Yes - hosted per-token is our public API price estimate (model dependent). For Dedicated we model GPUs (hours), expected utilization, licensing/overheads, and then amortize to get $/1k tokens. We'll include GPU type assumptions (A100 vs H100 vs Ada-like) in the SOW. Also include savings from batching and cache hit-rate assumptions.

[04:18] Tom: Can you give a ballpark? Without running our workloads, what's a rough hosted per-1k token for a trimmed model?

[04:26] Maya: Ballpark only - for a quantized 13B-like open model on hosted, maybe $0.015-0.03 per 1k tokens depending on batch/caching. Larger models or low-batching scenarios hit higher. We'll validate with your actual prompts.

[04:45] Carlos: To be concrete in the POC we'll run three benchmark profiles you provide: 1) short chat (avg 250 tokens), 2) standard analysis (avg 1.2k tokens), 3) long summarization (avg 3.5-4k tokens). We'll measure latency distributions at concurrency levels that map to your 120 concurrent sessions and 1k concurrent burst tests.

[05:10] Lena: For benchmarking data we'll share a 7-day token histogram and a sample of 200 representative prompts per profile. We'll scrub PII.

[05:25] Maya: Perfect. We'll also ask for targets per profile - is the 300ms p50 / 900ms p95 across all three or just the critical endpoint?

[05:33] Tom: Critical endpoint is the short chat - for long summarization longer latency is acceptable, p95 under 2.5s is fine for that path.

[05:44] Carlos: Noted. Now about caching: if you have a repeated system prompt and similar left context we typically see 20-60% token cost reduction for applicable calls. But depends on hit rate. For modeling, provide expected cache hit-rate or we'll assume conservative 25% and an optimistic 55% scenario.

[06:05] Priya: Are there extra costs or limits for caching in hosted mode?

[06:10] Carlos: No extra charge, it's a runtime optimization. The cost benefit is in fewer tokens processed by the model; you still pay per token for what gets executed. For Dedicated, you can configure larger KV caches and persistent workers to get better performance and lower per-token cost at high utilization.

[06:28] Maya: We should talk about cold starts and burst policy - with hosted we'll auto-burst but p95 can spike. Dedicated gives more predictable throughput with reserved capacity pricing. We'll show both scenarios in the pricing sheet.

[06:44] Tom: Leadership cares about predictable monthly spend. How do you model tail utilization and overprovisioning for Dedicated?

[06:52] Carlos: For Dedicated we estimate required GPU hours from expected QPS, tokens/second and latency SLO. Then propose a commit level (e.g., 2x baseline capacity) to handle peaks, and optional burst pool. We'll provide sensitivity analysis: utilization 40% vs 70% impacts $/1k tokens a lot.

[07:14] Lena: Quick question: what's the typical batch size you see in production? Will high batch sizes break the latency SLO?

[07:21] Carlos: Batch sizes are dynamic; we use continuous batching and cap latency impact. For sub-300ms p50 targets, we typically set max batch wait ~10-20ms and rely on concurrency to fill batches; effective batch sizes of 8-32 are common depending on traffic pattern. If you need strict single-digit-ms latency, batching less effective.

[07:43] Maya: For the POC we can test varying batch wait windows and quantify the latency vs cost tradeoff. We'll include a chart mapping batch wait to p95 latency and $/1k tokens.

[07:55] Priya: On security - we need SOC2, SSO, audit logs, KMS for keys, and an option for VPC/private deployment. Are those available for POC?

[08:05] Maya: Yes - we have SOC2 material and SSO support; for POC we can provide a private VPC trial environment (short-lived) or hosted with strict data retention policies. We'll attach security docs. Carlos will follow up with specifics on KMS integration and audit logs.

[08:23] Carlos: For on-prem or VPC we ship a private control plane option; that adds setup time. For the POC timeline (6 weeks) hosted tests are fastest - we can emulate VPC constraints in hosted but full private deployment typically extends timeline to 8-12 weeks.

[08:42] Tom: Timeline question - how long to run benchmarks and get results?

[08:46] Maya: Rough plan: week 0 (this week) share samples and SOW; week 1 run hosted benchmarks; week 2 analyze and tune batching/caching; week 3 show results and propose Dedicated sizing if needed; aim to conclude by week 6 with final recommendation. So roughly a 4-6 week engagement depending on scope.

[09:08] Lena: Sounds good. On metrics - please include p50/p95 latency, throughput (tokens/sec), GPU utilization (for dedicated), and per-1k token cost.

[09:18] Carlos: We'll capture those. For per-token cost we'll present three curves: naive (no caching, batch size 1), moderate (batch size 8, cache 25% hit), and optimized (batch 16-32, cache 50%+). That will materialize into $/1k token estimates.

[09:36] Priya: How are model updates handled? If we switch model versions during POC, does that impact cost projections?

[09:42] Carlos: Yes - model family, quantization, and sequence length all affect kernel throughput. We'll stick to 2 model families for the POC: a 7-8B quantized option and a 13-14B quantized option so you can compare quality vs cost.

[09:58] Tom: Any concerns about hallucination/regression when moving to smaller quantized models? We care about accuracy tradeoffs too.

[10:06] Maya: We'll tie cost to quality - include evaluation prompts and quality thresholds as part of success criteria. If optimized scenario reduces cost but fails quality checks, that would not meet acceptance.

[10:20] Lena: Ok. One practical: what artifacts will you need from us for the benchmark runner?

[10:25] Carlos: A token histogram, 200 representative prompts per profile, expected concurrency and traffic pattern (RPS over time). Also credentials for a test workspace (we can generate ephemeral keys) and your security contact.

[10:36] Tom: We'll get that over by Monday.

[10:40] Maya: Great. I'm going to summarize next steps - and then open for any final clarifications.

[10:46] Maya: Summary: Redwood will send SOW and pricing scenarios; SE will run three benchmark profiles on hosted and return raw logs; Aperture will provide prompts and histograms; security docs will be shared; schedule a follow-up deep-dive for quantization tuning.

[11:02] Priya: One last ask - include a sensitivity table showing $/1k tokens at utilization points 30%, 50%, 70% for Dedicated. That helps procurement.

[11:12] Carlos: Will do. We'll include model selection assumptions, GPU types, and batching/cache hit-rate assumptions in the table.

[11:20] Tom: Thanks team. Looking forward to the SOW.

[11:24] Maya: Thanks all, we'll follow up with calendar invites for the deep-dive.

[11:28] (Call ends)
